newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FEATURE-Aussie businessman heads for U.S. roasting.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Aussie businessman heads for U.S. roasting.

text.p: Sam Linz, a latter-day business adventurer, is about to follow in the footsteps of Marco Polo by igniting a culinary debate that could span the ages.
Italian explorer Marco Polo made a return trip to China 700 years ago and set off a dispute on the origin of pasta still raging among kitchen buffs who can spell "al dente".
Now Linz has plans for the United States which could raise a similar, burning question -- who invented the barbecue?
WHO KNOWS WHERE THE FIRST STEAK WAS GRILLED?

"In Australia, we like to think the barbecue was invented by us. But in the States they also claim the first one," said Linz, who runs Barbecues Galore, Australia's only dedicated chain of barbecue stores.
His privately held Australian company is now planning an expansion in the U.S. market which could see up to 400 Barbecues Galore stores stateside in the next decade.

In an interview with Reuters, Linz said the expansion would probably be based on a NASDAQ listing in the next 12 months that would give investors a 30-40 percent stake in a company which already has 35 profitable stores in California, Nevada, Arizona, Texas, Georgia, and Florida.
"We also have to get into New York and the East Coast," he says, claiming that this region had more weekend chefs (nearly always male) than the rest of the nation.
U.S. OPERATION HAS NO DIRECT RIVAL

The U.S. stores are "niche category-killers", according to the South African-born businessman, with large free-standing shops which sell nothing but barbecues, sauces, tongs, aprons and accessories needed to cook good meat.
While there is no direct competition for Barbecues Galore in the United States, retailers such as Sears Roebuck and Home Depot have sections devoted to barbecues and provide some rivalry.
Linz and his three partners in the Sydney-based Galore Group opened the first U.S. store 15 years ago but the operation has only begun turning a profit in the past few years.
"U.S. fund managers focus on quarterly performance and we have just begun the U.S. barbecue season. Early indications are positive in the lead-up to the IPO (initial public offering)."

A leading Wall Street investment bank, which he won't name, has offered to support the IPO based on the growth outlook for the U.S. stores, and subject to the Dow index holding up for the next year or so. Linz hopes to raise US$30 million to US$40 million from the share offer.
SALES ARE HOTTING UP
While he would not reveal profits, Linz said the U.S. stores had sales of A$32 million (US$25 million) in 1996 and this was expected to rise to A$50 million this year.
The U.S. stores are run by Sydney Selati, who left South Africa with Linz in 1980 but made his home in the United States instead of Australia.

"The early days in the States were difficult. First we had one store and then we had three for a number of years. We now have the infrastructure in place -- Australian manufacturing, computers, trained staff -- to make sure the operation is on a sure footing," Linz said.
EARLY DAYS WERE DIFFICULT
Linz, who ran a chain of liquor stores in South Africa but found apartheid too much to handle, also found the early days in Australia less than easy.

The Galore Group was listed on the Australian share market but taken private in 1996 after a few years of lacklustre performance which was largely affected by unsuccessful diversifications in Australia and the United States.
Linz says the lessons have been learnt, but the question of who lit the first barbecue may never be answered.
MAYBE THE FRENCH WERE FIRST
There is not a large body of research available on the outdoor cooking industry.

But for those who are interested, the word barbecue is usually considered to be derived from the French "barbe-a-queue" -- "from whiskers to tail". An ageing American encyclopedia claims the cooking of whole animals on an outdoor roast was introduced to America by French hunters before independence.

Ross McDonald, the boss in Australia of U.S. barbecue manufacturer Weber, has another theory. "The Aborigines might have been the first barbecuers," he says of Australia's indigenous hunter-gatherers. (A$1 = US$0.78)
